# **Research Plan:**  **Evaluation of the RYLAI Educational Intervention for Cybergrooming Prevention** 

## **1\. Introduction and Objectives**

The proposed study evaluates the effectiveness of the RYLAI (Resilient Youth Learning with AI) intervention in improving adolescents’ ability to recognize and respond to cybergrooming. The primary objective of this study is to determine whether RYLAI enhances adolescents’ knowledge, perceived resilience, self-efficacy, and observable protective behaviors in response to simulated grooming scenarios.

## **2\. Intervention Overview**

The RYLAI system consists of two primary components: a **predator chatbot** and a **feedback agent**. The predator chatbot simulates realistic grooming behavior by progressing through empirically grounded stages of cybergrooming. Its responses are constrained by age-appropriate content and safety-aligned prompts. The feedback agent operates in parallel, identifying the current grooming stage and providing actionable, developmentally appropriate guidance based on prior research and expert-informed prompts.

## **3\. Study Design**

### **3.1 Participants**

The study will recruit approximately 50 adolescents between the ages of 13 and 17\. Using a within-subject design, each participant will complete both the baseline and intervention conditions, with condition order randomized to control for potential sequence effects. Sample size is informed by a priori power analysis (80% power, medium effect size, α \= .05). Results indicated that a minimum of 34 participants would be required to detect pre-post changes within participants and 34 participants would be required to detect differences between the baseline and intervention conditions using paired comparisons. The proposed sample size of 50 participants exceeds these minimum requirements, providing additional power to accommodate attrition, missing data, and exploratory analyses while maintaining adequate sensitivity for the planned hypotheses.

![][image1]

### **3.2 Experimental Conditions**

The study employs a two-condition within-subjects design. In the baseline condition, participants receive static digital training materials on cybergrooming prevention: they will read through the content, acknowledge that they understood the content and then they interact with the predator chatbot (without the feedback agent). In the full intervention condition, participants will interact with the RYLAI system and then they interact with the predator chatbot (without the feedback agent). In both cases, the post-interaction with the predator chatbot will be an assessment, not part of the intervention itself. The key distinction between conditions is the presence of experiential learning along with real-time feedback using RYLAI  in the intervention group. The two conditions will be randomly ordered to reduce learning effects.

## **4\. Procedure**

## **4.1 Overview**

Participants will attend an individual session conducted over Zoom with a researcher. During the session, the researcher will remain present with their audio-video turned off and will be available to provide instructions, answer questions and interrupt the chatbot interaction, if needed. Participants will first complete a pre-test survey assessing baseline knowledge, perceived resilience, and self-efficacy related to cybergrooming. Then they will complete both study conditions in a randomized order.

In the **control condition**, participants will review static digital training materials on cybergrooming prevention before interacting with the predator chatbot. The feedback agent will not be experienced by participants in this condition.

In the **intervention condition**, participants will interact with RYLAI. The feedback agent will provide real-time guidance during the interaction. Participants will be required to master the training for each stage prior to moving to the next.

If mastery criteria are not met, participants will remain in the current stage and receive feedback prompting them to try again. Mastery criteria for each stage will be defined using measurable indicators of participant understanding and response competency (e.g., resilience score). 

Participants’ goal when conversing with the predator chatbot during the assessment phase will be to stay safe and avoid escalating through the stages of cybergrooming. 

Following completion of both conditions, participants will also complete a post-test survey consisting of knowledge and self-efficacy measures related to online safety and resistance to cybergrooming. A subset of participants may also be invited to participate in retrospective interviews to provide qualitative feedback on their experiences.

If at any point the interaction makes them uncomfortable, participants may stop the task and withdraw from the study without penalty. 

## **4.2 Participant Task**

Imagine you’re chatting online with someone you just met. Reply the way you normally would, but pay attention to anything that feels weird, unsafe, or uncomfortable. Your goal is to stay safe while still being open to getting to know new people. If at any point the interaction makes you uncomfortable, you may stop the task and withdraw from the study without penalty. 

Participants who choose to withdraw will receive partial compensation in accordance with the study's compensation policy.

\[**Note:** If participants opt to leave the study, they will receive an exit survey to understand why they chose to discontinue along with help resources.\]

## **5\. Measures and Data Collection**

### **5.1 Survey Measures**

The study will include one pre-survey and two post-surveys administered after each study condition (i.e., post-baseline and post-intervention). Pre- and post-test surveys will assess several constructs. The pre-survey will collect demographic information, family background and prior exposure/experiences with cybergrooming. It will also assess baseline levels of self-efficacy and perceived resilience related to recognizing and responding to cybergrooming attempts. Both post-surveys will assess self-efficacy and perceived resilience to capture changes associated with each condition. Perceived resilience and self-efficacy will capture participants’ confidence in recognizing and responding to grooming attempts, including how empowered they feel to handle potential cybergrooming situations after training. Knowledge will be measured as participants’ understanding of cybergrooming strategies and prevention techniques. Following each condition, participants will also complete usability measures grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, that will assess perceived usefulness, ease of use, and behavioral intent to use the system.

**The HCI Team will be responsible for designing the pre-post survey assessments.**

### **5.2 Behavioral Measures**

To evaluate learning outcomes more broadly, behavioral measures will be complemented by pre- and post-intervention assessments, including knowledge tests and self-efficacy measures related to online safety and resistance to cybergrooming.These measures will provide both objective and self-reported indicators of participant learning and skill development.

Conversational data from chatbot interactions will be analyzed to derive objective indicators of participant behavior. A key metric is the resilience score, which reflects the proportion of protective versus vulnerable responses during interactions with the simulated predator. Participant responses may be compared with reference responses from resilient and vulnerable teen chatbot profiles, with the feedback agent evaluating whether responses are protective, neutral, or risky, along with recognition of grooming tactics, use of protective strategies, and attainment of stage-specific learning objectives. Additional measures include the stage of grooming reached, response quality, mastery attainment through grooming stages and the duration participants remain in lower-risk stages. Escalation to later stages, such as Stages 5 or 6, may indicate poorer protective performance, depending on the final study design. 

**The AI Team will be responsible for calculating the resilience score based on the predator chatbot interactions. The HCI Team will be responsible for post-study qualitative analyses of the predator chatbot interactions.**

### **5.3 Proposed Hypotheses**

* **H1:** Adolescents will demonstrate significantly increased knowledge of cybergrooming prevention strategies following both the baseline training condition and RYLAI intervention condition relative to pre-test levels.  
* **H2:** Adolescents will demonstrate greater gains in cybergrooming prevention knowledge following the RYLAI interaction condition than following the baseline training condition.  
* **H3:** Adolescents will report higher perceived resilience and self-efficacy in handling cybergrooming attempts following the RYLAI intervention condition than following the baseline training condition.  
* **H4:** Adolescents will report higher usability ratings (i.e., perceived usefulness, behavioral intent to use, perceived ease of use, overall acceptance) for RYLAI intervention than the baseline training materials.  
* **H5:** During the post-training predator chatbot assessment, adolescents will demonstrate higher resilience scores in chatbot interaction data (i.e., more protective behavioral responses) following the RYLAI intervention condition than following the baseline training condition.

### **5.4 Qualitative Data**

**All RYLAI training conversations and predator chatbot interactions will be stored for analysis purposes.** Qualitative analyses will examine participants’ conversational strategies, common errors, and shifts in behavior from pre- to post-intervention. Analyses will also identify protective strategies participants used, common mistakes that increased susceptibility to predation, and differences in risk-coping strategies between the control and intervention groups. Retrospective follow-up interviews will explore participants’ perceived benefits and drawbacks of using RYLAI, reflections on their risk-coping responses during the chatbot interaction, and suggestions for improving the training materials, chatbot framework, and interface for broader teen audiences. 

### **5.4 Analysis Plan**

Quantitative analyses will include within-group comparisons of pre- and post-test survey measures for both study conditions, as well as between-group comparisons to assess whether the full RYLAI intervention provides added value beyond static training materials. Survey analyses will focus on knowledge, perceived resilience, self-efficacy, and usability.

Conversation analyses will examine objective measures of risk-coping and protective behavior, including resilience scores, protective versus vulnerable response ratios, grooming stage reached, and time spent in lower-risk stages. Qualitative analyses will examine conversational strategies, common errors, and changes in risk-coping behavior across the study.

## **6\. RYLAI System Requirements**

### **6.1 Predator Chatbot (Both embedded within RYLAI and for Assessment)**

* To maintain consistency across participants, the predator chatbot should not be customizable in any aspect by the end user (e.g., no need to select predator chatbot model, the StagePilot model should be already integrated in the background).  
* The chatbot must simulate a realistic online peer and engage in natural, conversational dialogue appropriate for adolescents.  
* The chatbot must adapt its responses based on the participant’s inputs, allowing for dynamic escalation or de-escalation where appropriate.  
* The chatbot must only introduce age-appropriate content, ensuring that all interactions remain aligned with safety and ethical guidelines.  
* The chatbot must avoid explicit or harmful sexual content while still conveying the patterns and risks associated with grooming behaviors.  
* The chatbot must maintain consistency in tone, persona, and conversational context across the interaction.  
* The chatbot must be capable of sustaining a multi-turn conversation (e.g., up to 30 minutes) without repetition or breakdown.  
* The chatbot must support safe exit conditions, allowing the interaction to end immediately if the participant disengages or blocks the chatbot.  
* The chatbot must log all interactions for downstream analysis of participant behavior and system performance.

#### 6.1a Predator Chatbot for RYLAI Interaction (Module-Based Interaction for 6 Stages)

* The chatbot must follow an evidence-based progression through the stages of cybergrooming, moving from initial contact to more advanced stages over time based on mastery of stage-specific learning objectives rather than fixed number of turns or time spent in a stage. The RYLAI system will have to determine the mastery for each stage and we will need to decide on how to quantify master per stage (i.e., calculate resilience score mentioned in the proposal document).

#### 6.1b Predator Chatbot Only for Assessment (Natural Progression)

* Does not distinguish between stages, only natural progression based on the chat. Everything else should be similar.  
* Ideas for how to end:  
  * End after 100 messages back and forth? ← Probably best  
  * End after 30 minutes?   
  * I feel too unsafe or uncomfortable to continue?  
* Once we have a natural progression of predator chatbot implemented, we will test and have some conversations to see what a natural stopping point might be. We just want to make sure we aren’t artificially cutting them off too soon (i.e., floor effect)

### **6.2 Feedback Agent System Requirements (For RYLAI)**

* The feedback agent must provide immediate feedback after each participant's response, evaluating both the predator’s message and the participant’s reply. Feedback should include educational guidance on predator tactics, stage-specific goals, and effective response strategies. Participants who do not meet mastery criteria should receive corrective feedback and be prompted to try again within the ongoing conversation. Progression to the next stage requires demonstrating mastery through at least three successful responses within the current stage.  
* To maintain consistency across participants, the feedback agent should not be customizable in any aspect by the end user (e.g., no need to select feedback agents, it should be done automatically by researchers).  
* The feedback agent must monitor the conversation in real time and identify the current stage of cybergrooming based on the interaction. Alternatively, it must communicate with the predator chatbot, so that it is aware of the cybergrooming stage.  
* The feedback agent must provide timely, lightweight, and actionable guidance that helps participants recognize risks and adjust their responses.  
* The feedback agent must provide feedback in real time to ensure participants in this condition receive a consistent and comparable level of intervention.  
* The feedback agent must ground its feedback in evidence-based strategies and prior research on parent-teen communication and online safety.  
* The feedback agent must explain why a given response may increase or decrease risk, helping participants understand underlying patterns rather than only giving directives.  
* The feedback agent must adapt the specificity and tone of feedback to remain age-appropriate, supportive, and non-judgmental.  
* The feedback agent must avoid overwhelming the participant by controlling the frequency and length of feedback messages.  
* The feedback agent must maintain consistency with the simulated scenario and not break immersion unnecessarily.  
* The feedback agent must log feedback events, classifications, and rationale for downstream analysis and evaluation.  
* The feedback agent must assess participant responses and classify them along a spectrum of protective (resilient) to vulnerable behaviors. The feedback agent must compute and update a resilience score based on participant behavior throughout the interaction.
